Field surveys of the Four-spotted goby (Deltentosteus quadrimaculatus) in the eastern Adriatic Sea have provided detailed morphometric data across multiple life stages. The maximum recorded total length for this cryptobenthic species reaches 10.3 cm [Li = 10.3 cm], a size achieved by only the oldest individuals in the population. Analysis of gonadal development in preserved specimens indicates that the total length at which 50% of individuals attain sexual maturity is 6.2 cm [Lp = 6.2 cm], a benchmark commonly used to define the onset of the pubertal transition in small gobiid fishes. This size corresponds closely to a wet weight at puberty of 1.94 grams [Wwp = 1.94 grams], a value derived from length-weight regressions fitted to local capture records. These morphometric thresholds are notably lower than those reported for sympatric congeners, suggesting a relatively early maturation schedule that may be linked to elevated natural mortality rates in the shallow, structurally complex seagrass beds that constitute its primary habitat.

The reproductive ecology of the Four-spotted goby is characterized by a modest but sustained output facilitated by repeated spawning events across a single breeding season. Females produce clutches containing a small number of eggs per clutch, and they typically complete multiple nesting cycles throughout the spring and summer months, generating approximately four to five clutches per year [F_R_i = approximately four to five clutches per year]. This reproductive strategy, involving batch spawning over an extended period, is common among small-bodied gobiids inhabiting temperate coastal zones where seasonal productivity is high but predictable. The maximum reproductive rate, derived from studies on the related Rhinogobius brunneus, has been estimated under controlled thermal conditions; at a stable water temperature of 15.2 °C [T = 15.2 °C], the daily egg output can approach a rate of approximately 4.7 eggs per day, reflecting an upper physiological limit constrained by somatic energy reserves and ovarian capacity.

Early life history traits of the Four-spotted goby reflect a high degree of parental investment relative to egg size, a pattern observed across several gobiid lineages. Newly hatched larvae emerge from demersal clutches at a remarkably small wet weight at birth of 0.0002771 grams [Wwb = 0.0002771 grams], a value consistent with the small egg dimensions (approximately 1.08 mm in length by 0.70 mm in width) typical of the genus Pomatoschistus. Under laboratory incubation conditions held at 15.2 °C [T = 15.2 °C], the age at birth, from oviposition to chorion rupture, is approximately 12 days [ab = approximately 12 days]. This relatively short embryonic period facilitates rapid yolk-sac depletion and the transition to exogenous feeding, a critical window during which larval survival is heavily dependent on the pulsed availability of microzooplankton in the pelagic environment. The combination of minute larval size and brief incubation likely shapes the species' colonization dynamics in fragmented coastal habitats.

As the Four-spotted goby progresses through its juvenile phase, somatic growth accelerates until individuals approach their asymptotic dimensions. The ultimate wet weight, representing the maximum body mass attained by fully grown adults in local populations, has been recorded at 9.33 grams [Wwi = 9.33 grams], a value that places the species among the smaller members of the sand-dwelling gobiid guild in the Adriatic Sea. This value, combined with an ultimate total length of 10.3 cm, yields a robust body shape index consistent with a benthic, ambush-feeding lifestyle. Comparative morphometric analysis with other sand-dwelling gobiids suggests that Deltentosteus quadrimaculatus falls toward the lower end of the size spectrum within its guild, a position that constrains its competitive interactions for both food resources and nesting crevices. Field observations indicate that individuals rarely exceed this ceiling mass, and senescence-related declines in body condition become apparent only in the oldest members of the cohort.

Longevity records for the Four-spotted goby, based on mark-recapture studies conducted in the northern Adriatic at a mean annual water temperature of 15.2 °C [T = 15.2 °C], indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 6 years [am = approximately 6 years]. This extended lifespan is notable among small gobiids, many of which are annual or biennial, and it may be facilitated by the species' iteroparous spawning schedule and relatively low metabolic demands associated with cool, stable thermal regimes. The combination of a maximum lifespan of 6 years [am = 6 years] with a reproductive strategy yielding multiple clutches per year suggests that lifetime fecundity can accumulate substantially, even if individual clutch sizes remain modest at a temperature of 15.2 °C [T = 15.2 °C]. Such a life-history configuration aligns with predictions for a species occupying a low-predation, resource-predictable environment where steady, repeated reproduction outweighs the benefits of a single, high-investment spawning event. Future demographic studies should investigate whether this longevity holds across the species' full geographic range.
